newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-ANTON WINS SPANISH DUEL TO TAKE MARATHON GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ANTON WINS SPANISH DUEL TO TAKE MARATHON GOLD.

text.p: Abel Anton deprived fellow Spaniard Martin Fiz of a second consecutive world title when he took the marathon gold after an exciting finale on Sunday.

Anton, the 10,000 metres European champion, used his track speed to outsprint Fiz just before the leading pair entered the Panathinaikon stadium, site of the 1896 Olympic Games, where the finish was decided.
The winner covered the 42.195 kms ancient course from Marathon to Athens in two hours 13 minutes 16 seconds on a hot, sunny morning.

Fiz, who had chosen to wear the same white running shoes which helped him to victory two years ago in Gothenburg, crossed the line just behind in 2:13.21. Commonwealth champion Steve Moneghetti of Australia was a distant third in 2:14.16.
Anton and Fiz escaped from a group of 10 runners after some 25 kilometres, in the hilliest part of the course.
The 34-year-old Anton, who made a brilliant marathon debut after a long career on the track when he won in Berlin last year, let Fiz do all the hard work until the last few hundred metres.
The two had the marble columns of the Panathinaikon stadium's entrance in sight when Anton moved past his compatriot, who could not find the strength to react.
"With one kilometre to go, I knew I was going to win because I was the faster runner," said Anton after completing only his third marathon.
Jean-Paul Gahimbare of Burundi led for most of the first 10 kilometres of the race, based on the historic run of messenger Phidippides in 490 B.C.
Willy Kalombo of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Luketz Swartbooi of Namibia then broke away, soon joined by Spaniard Fabian Roncero.
A group of seven runners including the eventual medalists closed the gap on the leading trio halfway through the course. Fiz attacked shortly after and only Anton was able to follow.

"He (Fiz) spoke to me a couple of time, telling me he wanted to go faster and asking me to cooperate," Anton said. "I told him I didn't want to go faster and just wanted to run my own race. He said he understood."
Fiz suffered dehydration from the stifling heat in the last few kilometres and did not attend the post-race news conference.
The 34-year-old Moneghetti, who has been a top class marathon runner for the last 10 years, decided to run at his own pace rather than waste energy trying to catch the Spanish duo.

"Those are my fifth world championships and my fourth in the marathon," said the veteran Australian, who enjoyed his best result with a fourth place in 1987 and tried his luck over 10,000 metres in 1993.
"I realised before the race that these were probably my last championships and I said to myself: 'You'd better get a medal here'."
